data.title: How we pack a daypack for a long day out
data.excerpt: A simple order for loading a daypack so the things you need are never at the bottom.
data.photo_alt: Dark green daypack on a rocky ridge

children.text: Heavy items sit close to your back and mid-height, light items go at the bottom, and anything you may need quickly lives in the lid or a side pocket.
Keep rain gear and a warm layer together near the top. Small items such as a headlamp and first-aid kit go in one labelled pouch so you can find them without unpacking.

data.title: Layering for cold mornings on the trail
data.excerpt: Three layers, one rule: start slightly cool and add layers at the first stop.
data.photo_alt: Green down jacket on a rocky outcrop

children.text: A base layer manages moisture, a mid layer adds warmth and a shell blocks wind and rain. Starting a little cool means you will not overheat in the first mile.
Stop at the first viewpoint to adjust. Taking a layer off before you sweat is easier than drying out after.

data.title: Stove care basics for the season
data.excerpt: A few minutes of cleaning and a leak check keep a canister stove dependable.
data.photo_alt: Black camping stove on a rock with blurred mountains behind

children.text: Check the O-ring for cracks, wipe grit from the burner and test the igniter at home rather than on the trail.
Store canisters upright and dry, and keep a lighter as a backup.

data.title: Osprey Exos 58 Review
data.summary: A lightweight thru-hiking favorite that keeps getting better.
data.author: Alex Carter
data.lead: The Osprey Exos 58 continues to be one of the most popular lightweight backpacks for long-distance hikers, and for good reason. It strikes an impressive balance between low weight, all-day comfort and real-world durability. After testing it on a range of trips, here’s how it performs.
data.pros:
Exceptionally lightweight for its capacity
Comfortable carry, even on long days
Well-ventilated back panel
Simple, streamlined feature set
Proven reliability on long-distance trails
data.cons:
Minimal padding on hip belt
Not ideal for very heavy loads
Side pockets can be tricky to access while moving
Fewer organization options than heavier packs
data.specs:
Capacity | 58 liters (M/L)
Weight (claimed) | 2 lb 10 oz (1.19 kg)
Torso sizes | S/M, M/L
Load range | Up to 30 lbs (14 kg)
Frame | Internal, tensioned mesh
Material | 100D recycled nylon
Hydration compatible | Yes
Rain cover | Not included
Sizes | S/M, M/L

sections.heading: A closer look
sections.body: The Osprey Exos 58 is designed for hikers who want to cover big miles with a light and comfortable pack. The latest version refines an already proven formula with improved materials and a more stable carry, while keeping the weight impressively low. It’s a great option for thru-hikes, week-long trips and anyone who values simplicity and efficiency.

sections.heading: Performance
sections.body: With a light load the frame disappears and the pack moves with you. The tensioned mesh back panel keeps a gap between the pack and your back, which helps on warm climbs. Push past the recommended load and the suspension starts to feel its limits, so this is a pack for people who have already trimmed their base weight.

sections.heading: Comfort & fit
sections.body: Two torso sizes keep the fit straightforward, and the shoulder straps are slim but supportive. The hip belt is the thinnest part of the design: it carries a light load well, but heavier loads would benefit from more padding.

sections.heading: Features
sections.body: A stretch front pocket, two side pockets, a removable top lid and a hydration sleeve cover the essentials. There is no built-in rain cover, so budget for one separately.

data.bottom_line: A light, comfortable pack that rewards a trimmed-down kit. If your loads stay under about 30 lbs, the Exos 58 is hard to fault; if you regularly carry more, look at a pack with a sturdier hip belt.
data.price_note: Reviewer’s noted price: about $260. Check the retailer for today’s price.

data.title: Salomon X Ultra 4 Review
data.summary: A versatile trail shoe that handles big miles with ease.
data.author: Jamie Park
data.lead: The X Ultra 4 sits between a trail runner and a hiking boot: more support than a running shoe, far lighter than a boot. This demo review looks at who it suits and where it asks for compromise.
data.pros:
Light and agile on rough ground
Grippy outsole on dry rock and dirt
Quick, secure lacing system
Comfortable out of the box
data.cons:
Standard version is not waterproof
Limited ankle support with a heavy pack
Toe box runs slightly narrow
data.specs:
Weight (pair, claimed) | about 1 lb 15 oz (880 g)
Heel-to-toe drop | 10 mm
Upper | Synthetic mesh with welded overlays
Outsole | Contagrip
Waterproof | Not in this version
Best for | Day hikes and light overnights

sections.heading: A closer look
sections.body: A low-cut shoe with a protective toe cap and a lacing system that cinches with one pull. It is built for hikers who prefer to move quickly over mixed terrain.

sections.heading: Performance
sections.body: On dry trails the outsole grips confidently. In wet conditions the mesh upper lets water in, so consider the waterproof version if your trips are often damp.

sections.heading: Comfort & fit
sections.body: Cushioning is firm rather than plush, and the heel holds well. Hikers with wide feet should try a pair before buying.

sections.heading: Features
sections.body: Quick-lace pocket, protective rand and a gusseted tongue that keeps small debris out.

data.bottom_line: A fast, comfortable shoe for day hikes and light overnights. Carry heavier loads or wade through wet ground often and a boot will serve you better.
data.photo_alt: Grey and black trail shoe on a rock with mountains in the distance

data.author: Taylor Kim
data.lead: A two-person backpacking tent that has stayed popular for years. This demo review weighs its livability against its packed weight.

Roomy interior for two
Quick, color-coded pitch
Stable in moderate wind
data.cons:
Heavier than ultralight tents

data.specs:
Capacity | 2 people
Packed weight (claimed) | about 3 lb 7 oz (1.56 kg)
Floor area | about 29 sq ft
Doors | 2
Poles | Aluminum, single hub

sections.heading: A closer look
sections.body: A freestanding, single-hub design with a symmetrical layout, so both sleepers get their own door and gear space.

sections.heading: Performance
sections.body: Pitching is simple even in fading light. Guy lines add stability when the wind picks up.

sections.heading: Comfort & fit
sections.body: The near-vertical walls give more usable room than the floor area suggests. Two sleepers with regular-width pads fit with a little to spare.

sections.heading: Features
sections.body: Interior pockets, a gear loft loop and two generous vestibules for boots and packs.

data.bottom_line: A dependable, comfortable shelter for two. If every ounce counts, an ultralight tent will save weight; otherwise this one is easy to live with.

sections.body: Quilted baffles and a close, athletic cut make it easy to layer. The fabric is soft and quiet.

sections.body: Plenty of warmth for cool evenings and early starts. Pair it with a shell if rain is likely.

sections.heading: Features

data.bottom_line: A layer most hikers will use more than they expect. Keep it dry and it will serve for seasons.

data.title: The best hiking backpacks for every adventure
data.card_title: The best hiking backpacks for every adventure
data.summary: From day hikes to thru-hikes, find the right pack for your next trip.
data.hero_lede: Three packs that cover long weekends to long trails, with the numbers side by side.
data.short_answer: Match the pack to the heaviest load you realistically carry: ultralight frames suit light kits, internal-frame packs suit most trips, and a sturdier suspension is worth the weight once loads climb past 30 lb. The three packs below sit at different points on that scale.

sections.heading: How to choose
sections.body: Start with capacity for your longest trip, then check the manufacturer’s recommended load range. Torso length matters more than height: measure it and compare to each pack’s fit range.

faqs.question: Is a lighter pack always better?
faqs.answer: Not if the pack is working against the load you carry. A lighter frame saves weight only when your kit is light too.

data.title: How to choose a tent
data.summary: Key features, trade-offs and our top picks for different trips and terrains.
data.hero_lede: Weight, space and weather protection pull in different directions. Here is how to balance them.
data.short_answer: Pick the smallest tent that still lets you sit up and keep gear dry. Then choose between freestanding comfort and lighter, trekking-pole designs based on how far you carry it.

sections.heading: Size and weight
sections.body: Add one person to the number you plan to sleep: a two-person tent is a snug fit for two and comfortable for one with gear. Vestibules matter as much as floor area.

sections.heading: Weather protection
sections.body: Three-season tents suit spring to fall. Look for a full-coverage fly, taped seams and guy-out points for wind.

data.title: How to choose a daypack
data.summary: Capacity, fit and materials, and four daypacks worth a look.
data.hero_lede: Find the right daypack for your hikes, from short local trails to full days in the mountains. We’ll break down what matters, how to choose, and our top picks.
data.short_answer: A great daypack is comfortable, fits your gear, and works for the way you hike. The right choice depends on your typical trip length, the gear you carry, and how you like a pack to fit. Below we break down the key factors to consider and recommend our favorite daypacks for a range of uses.

sections.heading: Daypack capacity
sections.body: Most day hikes fit in 18 to 28 liters. Go smaller for short, warm-weather walks and larger when you carry extra layers, food for the day or camera gear.

sections.heading: Fit and comfort
sections.body: Check torso length and choose a hip belt that sits on your hip bones. Padded shoulder straps and a ventilated back panel make long days easier.

sections.heading: Materials and features
sections.body: Ripstop nylon resists snags. Look for a hydration sleeve, stretch side pockets for bottles and a lid or zip pocket for small items.

sections.heading: How we choose
sections.body: We compare published specifications, fit options and features across brands, and we note where a claim comes from the maker. This page contains sample content for the theme and does not describe real testing.

faqs.question: What size daypack do I need?
faqs.answer: Between 18 and 28 liters covers most day hikes. Choose the lower end for warm, short outings and the upper end for cold weather or long days.

faqs.question: Should a daypack have a hip belt?
faqs.answer: For loads over about 10 lb a hip belt moves weight off your shoulders. For lighter loads a simple sternum strap may be enough.
